utterance: Just to be clear on two points, because they matter for your treatment: are you allergic to any antibiotic, for example penicillin or flucloxacillin? And did you have a cold, sore throat or feverish illness in the fortnight before this started?

utterance: Samuel, here's what I'm finding. Your pain started around the belly button and moved down to the right side, you've been sick, your appetite has gone, you have a fever of 37.9, your pulse is up at 102, and your tummy is very tender in the right lower side — it hurts when I press and let go, when you cough and even with the bumps in the car. That pattern points very strongly to inflammation of the appendix, which is called appendicitis. It's not something to watch and wait on — it needs a surgeon to see you today, usually within the next hour or two, and you may need an operation. So my plan is to send you straight to the emergency department. How did you get here today — did someone drive you, and is there someone who can take you now?
reply: That sounds pretty serious. My mate drove me here, but he had to head back to the site, so I will have to call my mum to come and get me.

utterance:
Samuel, let me explain clearly what I think is going on and what happens next.

What I found: your pain started around the belly button and settled in the right lower side of your tummy, you've lost your appetite, you've been sick, you have a temperature of 37.9 and a fast pulse of 102. On examination the tender spot is exactly where the appendix sits, and it hurts when I press and let go, when you cough, and with the bumps in the car — those are signs of irritation of the lining of the tummy. Your urine test and the examination of your testicles and your back rule out some of the other causes we always think about. All of this points strongly to an inflamed appendix — appendicitis.

What we're doing: I've already called an ambulance to take you to the emergency department now, rather than waiting for your mum, because this needs a surgeon to see you within the hour or two. I've also phoned the emergency department myself to hand over your story and my findings, so they'll be expecting you, and I'm sending your details and the blood tests I've taken (full blood count and CRP, which will confirm the inflammation). Please don't drive yourself anywhere.

At the hospital expect more bloods, probably a scan — an ultrasound or a CT — and a surgical review. If it is appendicitis, the usual treatment is a small keyhole operation to remove the appendix, plus antibiotics. It's a very common operation and people generally recover well. I've given you a gram of paracetamol for the pain just now; the paramedics and the hospital can give you stronger pain relief through a vein straight away — you should not have to tough this out.

Important while you wait: nothing to eat or drink at all — not even water, lollies or chewing gum — because you may need an anaesthetic. Don't take any laxatives or enemas, and don't take any more painkillers on top of what I've given.

One thing I want you to understand: if the pain suddenly eases a lot, that is not a sign you're better — it can mean the appendix has burst. So you must still go, whatever happens. And if the pain becomes much worse, spreads across the whole tummy, your tummy feels hard, you keep vomiting, you feel faint or your fever spikes before the ambulance gets here, tell the paramedics straight away — and if you were ever at home with those symptoms, call 000 again immediately rather than waiting.

You'll need some time off work as an apprentice — I'll organise a medical certificate for you and for your employer. Any questions before the ambulance arrives?
reply: An ambulance seems like a bit of a fuss, but if you reckon I need it, I will wait here for them.

utterance: That's the right call, and I'm sorry it's uncomfortable — but I'd much rather you were watched by a surgeon today than sitting at home with an appendix that could burst. I'll stay with you until the paramedics arrive. You can ring your mum and ask her to come straight to the emergency department instead of here, and bring your Medicare card. Once they've assessed you, the hospital team will take it from there, and you'll get proper pain relief very quickly.
reply: Right, I will call her now.
